heading: Where I started, and what changed.
intro: This isn’t a rags-to-riches story. It’s a story about what happens when a young person gets the right people around them — and what he does with it afterwards.

chapters.statement: I was one of the young people I now work with.
body: I grew up in Tower Hamlets, one of the most deprived boroughs in the country. Crime, gang violence and youth violence weren’t things I read about. They were the backdrop.
Some of my closest friends didn’t make it out. Some went to prison. Some we lost to mental health. None of them had the right support at the right time.

image.alt: Nahim on the streets of Poplar, East London
image.caption: Poplar. The same streets, then and now.

chapters.statement: “You won’t even have the skills to be a dustbin cleaner.”
body: That’s what a teacher told me, in front of my classmates, as I came to the end of my A Levels. My GCSEs had already gone badly. I’d failed, miserably, by my own account.
It wasn’t feedback. It was a verdict. I carried it for a long time — not because I believed it, but because I couldn’t understand why someone whose job was to inspire would choose to do the opposite.

chapters.statement: Then I lost a close friend to reckless driving. Everything changed.
body: I went back to college and retook my GCSEs while working three jobs. In 2009 I started a degree in Youth and Community Work at the University of East London.
I wanted to build a better future. Not just for me — for the people around me, and especially for the young people coming up behind me.

image.alt: Nahim as a young youth worker

chapters.statement: Fifteen years on the frontline. Most of it on the streets.
body: Youth services are the gateway for young people who don’t know what’s out there — mental health support, training, jobs, someone to talk to. If we don’t go to them, most will never come to us.

So I went to them. Detached youth work on the corners and estates of Poplar, often late at night and often in my own time. Building trust one ordinary moment at a time: showing up, remembering names, keeping promises.

image.alt: Nahim with young people at Spotlight youth service
image.caption: Spotlight, Poplar HARCA’s youth service.

chapters.statement: I found out about the MBE in the mosque, straight after Eid prayers.
body: For services to disadvantaged young people in Tower Hamlets. A borough I was told I’d amount to nothing in.

Since then: a master’s at UCL on a full scholarship, completed while working full time. An honorary doctorate in Youth and Community Work. A Lifetime Achievement Award. Four universities, from someone who once had no GCSEs to speak of.

chapters.statement: The words that were meant to crush me became fuel.
body: I still work in Tower Hamlets. I still do the work. And now I get to stand in front of rooms full of people and tell them what I know for certain: nobody is hard to reach. We just have to be the ones who go.

timeline.label: Grows up in Poplar, Tower Hamlets
